guides.title: Humanity in the Federation
guides.summary: How the setting's humans are described from outside, and why the Federation looks like them.

sections.heading: The Species That Kept Volunteering
sections.body: Humans in this setting are not the most advanced, the strongest, the longest-lived or the most disciplined species in known space, and every other civilisation is aware of it. What they are is relentlessly present. Humans turn up. They join things, propose things, volunteer for things, and are disproportionately represented in every institution that involves going somewhere nobody has been. Other species describe this in terms that are not always complimentary. Vulcans have called it emotional volatility mistaken for enthusiasm. Klingons regard it as a strange kind of courage in a species that is physically unimpressive. Ferengi consider it economically irrational. Romulans, characteristically, regard it as expansion that has not yet admitted what it is. The setting's own answer is curiosity, and it is fair-minded enough to let the accusations stand alongside. A species that spreads outward with confident intentions has a history worth being suspicious of, and humans in this setting have exactly that history.

sections.heading: What Changed
sections.body: Human history in the setting runs through a devastating world war, a period of collapse, and a recovery that only became possible after first contact demonstrated that the species was neither alone nor central. The material conditions that followed — abundant energy, matter synthesis, an end to material scarcity — removed the pressures that most human conflict had run on. The result is presented as a genuine transformation rather than a change of manners. Humans of this era do not work for money because there is none to work for; they do things because the alternative is doing nothing, and the setting insists that most people find that insufficient. Status still exists, attaching to accomplishment, craft and service. The setting is also honest that this is a claim, not a demonstration. Characters from outside routinely point out that human virtue is untested when nobody is hungry, and the stories that put humans under real pressure are precisely the ones that take the objection seriously.

sections.heading: The Federation's Accent
sections.body: The Federation is a coalition of many worlds and it speaks with a noticeably human accent. Earth hosts its capital, Starfleet's command structure and traditions are recognisably drawn from human naval practice, and the working language of the fleet is a human one. Member species notice. The setting treats this as a real problem rather than a compliment. A federation whose institutions were shaped by one member will keep producing decisions that feel natural to that member and arbitrary to everyone else, and the complaint is voiced by Vulcans, Andorians, Tellarites and Bajorans at different times and never satisfactorily answered. The defence usually offered — that humans supplied the mediating temperament the founding needed, being neither as rigid as one founder nor as combative as another — is plausible and also exactly what a dominant partner would say. The setting leaves the tension in place, which is more interesting than resolving it.

sections.heading: Why Humans Are the Viewpoint
sections.body: Structurally, humans are the setting's translation layer. A story about a wholly alien crew would need everything explained; a story with a human aboard can have the alien explained to them and therefore to the audience. Almost every long-running character dynamic in the setting runs on some version of that. It is also why the setting's humans are written as unremarkable on purpose. They are not chosen, not destined and not superior; they are the species that happened to be curious enough and lucky enough to get out, and their significance is entirely a matter of what they did after that. The optimism the setting is known for is a claim about this species specifically: that a people with a genuinely terrible record can become something else, that the change is available rather than exceptional, and that it takes a couple of centuries and a very hard century first. That is a more demanding kind of hope than the cheerful reputation suggests.

guides.title: The Q Continuum
guides.summary: Beings for whom the laws of physics are optional, and what a setting does with an opponent it cannot fight.

sections.heading: What They Are
sections.body: The Q are effectively omnipotent within the terms the setting uses: they alter matter, energy, space and time at will, appear and vanish without transit, and are not meaningfully bound by distance, causality or death. They belong to a collective referred to as the Continuum, which has its own politics, disputes and law, and which is far stranger than any of its members individually. They appear as humanoids by choice, because a form is easier to talk to than a phenomenon. Nothing about the appearance is real in any sense the observer would recognise, and the setting occasionally makes a point of that by having one drop the pretence. Encounters with them are not battles. Weapons do nothing, defences do nothing, and the only available responses are argument, refusal, endurance and — occasionally — being interesting enough that the Q decides to stop. That constraint is the whole reason they work as a device.

sections.heading: The Trial That Never Closes
sections.body: The Q's recurring interest in humanity is framed as a trial: an inquiry into whether the species deserves to keep expanding, conducted by a judge who changes the rules, invents the evidence and enjoys himself thoroughly. It is opened early and deliberately never concluded, the position being that the trial into whether a species is worthy is not the sort of proceeding that ends. The device lets the setting put its own optimism on the stand. A being who can do anything asking why a species with humanity's record should be allowed out is not an easy question to answer with a speech, and the answers the characters produce have to be demonstrated instead. It also lets the setting be tested by something other than a fleet. A Q encounter is a moral examination in the shape of a spectacle, and the resolution is always some version of a person refusing to become what the situation is inviting them to become.

sections.heading: Omnipotence With a Personality Problem
sections.body: What keeps the Q from being unusable is that they are not serene. They are bored, vain, capricious, lonely, and susceptible to being irritated — a set of failings that would be trivial in anyone else and are catastrophic in beings who can rewrite a solar system on a whim. The Continuum is portrayed as a civilisation that solved everything and then had nothing left to want. Its members have exhausted curiosity, and what remains is either the maintenance of order or the entertainment of interfering with people who still have questions. That is a genuinely bleak idea underneath the comedy, and the setting has been willing to look straight at it. Individual Q also disagree with one another, are subject to their own law, and can be stripped of their powers as punishment. A Q made mortal — obliged to eat, to sleep, to be afraid and to depend on people they have spent centuries patronising — is one of the setting's better ideas and the closest it comes to explaining why any of this matters to them.

sections.heading: Why an Unbeatable Antagonist Is Useful
sections.body: A setting built on competence needs something competence cannot touch. Every other problem in the format yields to preparation, engineering, negotiation or courage; the Q yield to none of those, which forces the writers to find a different kind of resolution and forces the characters to be right rather than clever. They also serve as the setting's licence to be strange. A Q can move a ship across the galaxy, stage a courtroom out of nothing, or drop a crew into their own history, and the format can follow without any of its usual constraints applying. The device is a permission slip. The risk is obvious and the setting mostly manages it: an omnipotent character can solve or cause anything, so overuse would make the rest meaningless. The discipline is that the Q never fix what the crew ought to fix, and their interventions consistently make things harder rather than easier — which keeps the crew's competence the thing that actually matters.

guides.title: The Founders and the Changelings
guides.summary: Shapeshifters who rule an empire out of fear, and the one of them raised among solids.

sections.heading: Liquid Life
sections.body: The Founders are shapeshifters — beings whose natural state is a liquid rather than a form, and who can take the shape of any object or creature they have studied closely enough. They do not disguise themselves so much as become the thing, which is a distinction that matters enormously to anyone trying to detect them. In their own state they exist as a merged whole called the Great Link: an ocean of individuals dissolved into one another, sharing thought, memory and identity directly. Emerging from it to take a solid form is described as a diminishment, and long separation from it as a genuine deprivation. A Founder alone among solids is, by their own account, living in a permanently reduced condition. They require periodic return to a liquid state to rest, which is the single reliable vulnerability in an otherwise undetectable species and the hinge of several plots.

sections.heading: An Empire Built on Fear
sections.body: The Founders rule the Dominion, and their governing principle is stated plainly: what you cannot control cannot be trusted. It is not a philosophy arrived at abstractly. Their history, as they tell it, is one of being hunted and feared by solids wherever they were found, and the empire is the answer they arrived at — order imposed permanently so that it can never happen again. The setting takes this seriously rather than offering it as an excuse. A people genuinely persecuted, who responded by conquering the galaxy's other half to be safe from it, is a recognisable and disturbing shape. Their conviction that they are the wronged party is sincere and never entirely wrong. The administration is delegated. A client species, engineered for the purpose, negotiates and governs; another, engineered for war and chemically dependent on a substance only the Founders supply, fights. Both are taught to regard their masters as gods, and both mostly do.

sections.heading: Detecting Them
sections.body: A species that can be anything makes paranoia rational, and the setting uses that as its primary weapon long before any shooting starts. If a Founder can replace anyone, then every institution becomes suspect, allies begin investigating each other, and security measures start doing more damage than infiltration would have. Countermeasures exist and are all uncomfortable. Blood screenings, which can be defeated. Detection by forcing a shift. Fields that prevent shapeshifting, which have to be installed everywhere and inconvenience everyone. The setting is clear that the most effective damage the Founders do is what their targets do to themselves in response. The deeper point is that the fear is not irrational. Replacement did happen, at senior levels, and the difficulty is that a proportionate response and a paranoid one look identical from inside.

sections.heading: The One Who Was Raised Outside
sections.body: The setting's most durable Founder material concerns one raised among solids, found as a specimen, studied, given a name that was originally a laboratory label, and grown into a person shaped entirely by a society his own kind despise. He works in law enforcement, which is either irony or the same instinct expressed differently, and the setting never quite says. His existence puts the Founders' argument to the test. The Great Link offers him belonging, the end of loneliness, and the company of the only others of his kind; accepting it means joining an empire committing atrocities. Refusing it means remaining permanently alone among people he loves and does not resemble. That is the choice the setting keeps returning to, and it declines to make it easy in either direction. His people are genuinely his people, their offer is genuinely what he wants, and what they are doing is genuinely unforgivable — three things that are all true at once.
